_about: Plain-language definitions shown when someone taps or hovers an underlined term (src/ui/Term.tsx). 'matches' lists the words that get underlined, in any capitalization; only the first one in each paragraph is underlined. Keep definitions short (under about 40 words), in the same plain voice as copy.json. They explain words, never give legal advice. Set 'verified' to true once a team member has checked the definition against its source.

terms.definition: A court order that tells a person to stay away from you and stop contacting, threatening, or hurting you. If they break it, police can arrest them.
The court form you fill out to ask a judge for something, like a protection order. It says who you are, who the other person is, and what happened.
The person who files the petition and asks for the order. If you are filing for yourself, that is you.
The person the petition is about. The order would be against them. The court's forms call them the Respondent.
An adult who files court papers for a child, because a child can't file alone. This is usually a parent or guardian.
To deliver court papers to a person in an official way, so the court knows they got them. Usually the sheriff or another adult does this, not you.
A set time in court when a judge listens to both sides and decides what to order. You can bring proof and people who saw what happened.
Without the other person there. A judge can issue an ex parte order from your petition alone, before the other person is told or a hearing is held.
A written statement that a person signs, swearing that it is true. Someone who saw or heard what happened can write one for the court.
Lying on purpose in something you swear or sign is true. It is a crime. That is why you sign that what you wrote in the petition is true.
A separate form (PO-0104) with your private details, like your home address. Only the court, the clerk, the prosecutor, and police see it. The other person does not get a copy.
A form (PNW-0102) that tells the clerk to keep certain papers, like the Confidential Form, out of the public court record.
The court office that takes and files court papers and keeps the court's records. Clerk staff can explain how to file, but they can't give legal advice.
The government lawyer who decides whether to bring criminal charges. You do not need the prosecutor to ask for a protection order.
An order a judge makes in a criminal case, telling the person charged not to contact the victim. It is separate from a protection order.
When the court ends a case or petition without granting an order. For example, a petition can be dismissed if no one comes to the hearing.
Disobeying a court order. If the other person breaks the order, the court can find them in contempt and punish them, for example with a fine or jail.
A copy of a court paper that the clerk stamps or signs to show it is a true copy of the original.
An order an employer can ask for to protect an employee from violence or threats at work. Only the employer can file for it.
When a family or household member hurts you, tries to or threatens to hurt you, makes you afraid of being hurt, forces you into sexual activity, or hurts an animal to scare or control you.

Harassing someone again and again in a way that would make most people feel scared, threatened, or intimidated, and that does make the victim feel that way. Following, watching, or showing up can count.
Repeated contact you did not want that would upset most people and did upset you. Calls, texts, messages, or showing up can count.
A sexual crime, like rape, sexual battery, or child molesting. The person does not need to be charged or convicted for you to ask for an order.
When an adult contacts a child again and again to gain the child's trust and prepare them for sexual activity.
